corpusNote: Democritus was one of the most prolific writers of antiquity — Diogenes Laertius, drawing on the 1st-century-CE scholar Thrasyllus, preserves a catalogue of some 60+ titles organised into thirteen tetralogies on the model of Plato's works. Almost none of it survives as text. What we have is roughly 300 fragments in Diels–Kranz, the great majority of them short ethical maxims (the so-called 'Democrates' collection and the Stobaeus gnomology), whose authenticity is individually contested. So Democritus presents the opposite problem to Thales: a vast, precisely catalogued corpus of titles, and a body of surviving quotation that barely overlaps with it.

referenceSystems.name: Diels–Kranz
referenceSystems.note: Democritus = DK 68 (Leucippus = DK 67). A = testimonia; B = fragments (B0a–B298, many being the ethical maxims); C = the doubtful 'Democrates' sayings.

referenceSystems.name: Thrasyllus catalogue
referenceSystems.note: The tetralogical arrangement preserved in Diogenes Laertius IX.45–49 — the primary evidence for the shape of the lost corpus.

referenceSystems.name: Luria
referenceSystems.note: S. Luria, Democritea (1970) — the fullest modern collection of fragments and testimonia, with a different and more inclusive numbering than DK.

referenceSystems.name: Laks–Most
referenceSystems.note: Early Greek Philosophy, Loeb (2016), vols. VI–VII (Atomists), covering Leucippus and Democritus together.

works.title: The Great World-System
works.extent: Lost. Title and a few reported doctrines only. Heads tetralogy III of the physical works.
citations: Theophrastus (via DL IX.41, attributing it to Leucippus)
works.transmission: Named in the Thrasyllus catalogue among Democritus' physical works. But Theophrastus and part of the tradition attributed the Great World-System to Leucippus, Democritus' teacher — one of the central instances of the 'Leucippus problem'.
works.authenticity: Disputed authorship — Democritus or Leucippus. The dispute is old: the two atomists' works were already hard to separate in antiquity, and Epicurus is said to have denied Leucippus existed at all.
works.summary: The comprehensive cosmology of atomism: infinite atoms of every shape moving in infinite void, colliding and interlocking to form innumerable worlds that come to be and pass away. The foundational statement of the system, if the attribution to Democritus holds.
translations: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers, 2nd ed. (1983), ch. 15–17
Taylor, The Atomists: Leucippus and Democritus (1999) — Toronto, full fragments in English
works.notes: The Leucippus/Democritus attribution problem is the atomist analogue of the Empedocles one-poem question — worth teaching as a case where authorship itself is the scholarly object.

works.title: The Little World-System

date.note: The work apparently gave a date placing its composition 730 years after the fall of Troy (DK 68 B5), one of the few internal datings in the Presocratics.

works.extent: Lost. Title, plus the internal dating notice.
works.transmission: Thrasyllus catalogue; Diodorus Siculus preserves what may be a summary of its anthropology.
works.authenticity: Attributed to Democritus, and here Democritus' own authorship is better secured — Diogenes distinguishes it from the Great World-System partly to keep the Leucippus attribution straight.
works.summary: Apparently a cosmology and anthropogony on a smaller scale, including an account of the origin of human society, language, and the arts from need — the source, probably via Democritus, of the 'progressivist' account of civilisation later found in Diodorus, Lucretius, and Vitruvius.

works.title: On Cheerfulness (On Contentment)
works.extent: Lost as a text, but its doctrine and probably several of its sentences survive among the ethical fragments. In tetralogy II (Ethics).
citations: Seneca, De Tranquillitate Animi (title translated as tranquillitas)
works.transmission: The title is in the Thrasyllus catalogue. Its central concept, euthymia, is reported by Diogenes Laertius IX.45 as Democritus' name for the goal of life, and Seneca took the treatise's title as the model for his own On Tranquillity of Mind. Many of the Stobaeus ethical fragments plausibly derive from it.
works.authenticity: The work is genuine; the attribution of specific surviving maxims to it is inference. The larger authenticity problem is the ethical fragments as a class — the 'Democrates' collection (DK C) is of doubtful ascription, and scholars dispute how much of the gnomology is really Democritean.
works.summary: Euthymia — 'good-spiritedness', cheerfulness, contentment — as the end of life: a stable and tranquil condition of the soul, undisturbed by fear or superstition, achieved through moderation and the right measure of pleasures. 'Happiness dwells not in flocks nor in gold; the soul is the dwelling-place of the guardian spirit' (B171). The first developed eudaimonist ethics before Socrates, and a direct ancestor of Epicurean ataraxia.
translations: Freeman, Ancilla to the Pre-Socratic Philosophers (1948) — public domain
works.notes: The most consequential of the ethical works: euthymia is the concept that connects Democritus to Hellenistic ethics. Worth pairing in the atlas with Epicurus' Letter to Menoeceus.

works.title: On Logic, or The Canon
works.extent: Lost. Title (in three books) and reported doctrine. In tetralogy VI.
citations: Sextus Empiricus, Adv. Math. VII.135–140 (B9, B11)
works.transmission: Thrasyllus catalogue; the epistemological doctrine preserved by Sextus Empiricus, our best source for Democritus' theory of knowledge.
works.authenticity: Genuine title. The associated fragments B9 and B11 are among the most securely attested and quoted.
works.summary: The distinction between 'legitimate' (genuine) and 'bastard' knowledge, and the sceptical undertow of atomist epistemology: 'By convention sweet, by convention bitter, by convention hot, by convention cold, by convention colour; but in reality atoms and void' (B9). 'In reality we know nothing, for truth is in the depths' (B117). The senses reach only the bastard knowledge; reason, reasoning from the sensible to the atomic, the genuine. Democritus reportedly staged a dialogue in which the senses reply to the intellect: 'Wretched mind, do you, who get your evidence from us, throw us down? Our overthrow is your fall' (B125).
works.notes: B9 is the single most quoted Democritean sentence and the origin of the primary/secondary quality distinction that runs through Galileo and Locke.

works.title: The Thrasyllan corpus (complete catalogue of titles)
works.extent: The catalogue names 13 tetralogies (52 titles) plus further ungrouped works — the fullest map of any lost Presocratic corpus. Essentially none of the texts survive.
works.transmission: Thrasyllus, the astrologer-scholar of Tiberius' court, catalogued Democritus' works into tetralogies exactly as he had Plato's; Diogenes Laertius reproduces the list.
works.authenticity: The catalogue is genuine as a 1st-century-CE scholarly artefact; how many of the titles are authentically Democritean, and how many accreted to his famous name (the magical and alchemical works especially), is uncertain. Thrasyllus himself flagged some as doubtful.
works.summary: ETHICS (Tetr. I–II): Pythagoras; On the Disposition of the Wise Man; On the Things in Hades; Tritogeneia; On Manly Virtue; Amalthea's Horn; On Cheerfulness; Ethical Commentaries. — PHYSICS (III–VI): Great World-System; Little World-System; Cosmography; On the Planets; On Nature; On the Nature of Man (On Flesh); On Mind; On the Senses; On Flavours; On Colours; On the Different Shapes (of atoms); On Changes of Shape; Confirmations; On Images; On Logic or Canon (3 bks); Problems. — MATHEMATICS (VII–IX): On the Difference of the Gnomon (On the Contact of Circle and Sphere); On Geometry; Geometrica; Numbers; On Irrational Lines and Solids (2 bks); Projections; The Great Year (Astronomy, a calendar); Contest of the Water-Clock; Description of the Heavens; Geography; Description of the Pole; Description of Rays. — MUSIC/LITERATURE (X–XI): On Rhythms and Harmony; On Poetry; On the Beauty of Verses; On Euphonious and Cacophonous Letters; On Homer; On Song; On Words; Names. — TECHNICAL (XII–XIII): Prognosis; On Diet; Medical Judgement; Causes concerning Seasons; Causes concerning Fire; Causes concerning Sounds; Causes concerning Seeds and Plants and Fruits; Causes concerning Animals (3 bks); Miscellaneous Causes; On the Magnet. Plus nine books On Causes and various ungrouped/suspect works.
translations: Hicks, Diogenes Laertius, Loeb (1925) — public domain
works.notes: This entry IS the corpus for teaching purposes — the breadth (ethics, physics, maths, music, medicine, agriculture, magnetism) is the point: Democritus was the encyclopaedist of the 5th century, the 'laughing philosopher', and Aristotle wrote a lost monograph on him. Represent the tetralogies in the atlas as the catalogue, not as 60 separate recoverable texts.

works.title: Testimonia (DK 68 A)
works.extent: Large A-section in DK 68; the main route to the physics.
citations: Aristotle, Metaphysics 985b4–20, De Generatione et Corruptione I.1–8, De Anima 403b–405a
Simplicius, In De Caelo, In Physica
works.transmission: Aristotle is the indispensable witness for atomism — he took Democritus more seriously than any other Presocratic and reports the system in detail while rejecting it. Theophrastus' De Sensibus is our fullest source for the theory of perception. Simplicius, Sextus, and the doxographers fill in.
works.authenticity: Not by Democritus; the standard base for reconstructing the physics, since the physical works themselves are lost.
works.summary: Atoms and void; atoms differing only in shape (rhysmos), arrangement (diathigē), and position (tropē) — Aristotle's famous ABC analogy; necessity (anankē) and the vortex, with no room for chance in the modern sense; perception by effluences (eidōla); the soul as spherical fire-atoms; the denial of teleology that made Democritus Aristotle's chief antagonist and Epicurus' chief inspiration.

excluded.title: On Sympathies and Antipathies / alchemical and magical works (Physica et Mystica etc.)
excluded.reason: A body of Hellenistic alchemical and magical writing circulated under Democritus' name; already suspect to Thrasyllus. Now attributed to 'Bolos of Mendes' (pseudo-Democritus), 2nd c. BCE.

excluded.title: The Golden Verses / various gnomologies under 'Democrates'
excluded.reason: The 'Democrates' maxim collection (DK 68 C) is of uncertain ascription and may conflate genuine Democritean sayings with later gnomic material.
